en.content:
Hong Kong is considering issuing 10,000 ride-hailing permits under a new framework, a development that may look technical on the surface but speaks to a broader policy question: how to balance innovation and convenience with orderly governance. After years of rapid growth in app-based transport, the city’s challenge is not whether on-demand mobility belongs here, but how to make its growth sustainable—commercially, operationally, and in the public interest.

A permit-based approach can, in principle, reduce the friction that arises when service expansion outpaces regulation. Clear licensing helps set baseline standards for drivers, insurance, vehicle conditions, and service accountability—important for passenger safety and for fair competition with traditional transport sectors. It can also support better data collection, allowing the government to calibrate supply to demand and reduce the risks of market instability, fare volatility, or “ghost” activity that undermines legitimate operators. In this sense, the goal should be to tighten the regulatory net without choking innovation.

At the same time, the policy will only earn public trust if it is implemented with transparency and responsiveness. If permits are awarded without clear criteria, or if enforcement is uneven, the system can be perceived as favouring certain players rather than protecting users. Hong Kong also needs to ensure that any licensing scheme complements existing traffic and labour policies, including how driver earnings and working conditions are monitored over time. The government’s most significant task is therefore to make the framework adaptable—willing to adjust permit numbers, service requirements, and enforcement practices as the market evolves.

In the broader context of Hong Kong’s governance philosophy—seeking pragmatic, rules-based management—this ride-hailing proposal is best judged by its outcomes: safer rides, fairer competition, fewer disputes, and improved service reliability. If the new framework can deliver those results while keeping the market open enough for healthy innovation, it will represent a constructive step forward rather than a bureaucratic constraint.
en.topic_title: Hong Kong gov’t mulls 10,000 ride-hailing permits under new framework, report says

zh.content:
今次社會最需關注嘅，係 Meta 移除假冒 INTERPOL、並針對香港詐騙受害者嘅廣告。表面係一單平台打擊騙案嘅「小事件」，但背後反映嘅係同一套老牌手法：利用國際執法機構嘅權威外殼，減低受害者嘅戒心，再以「程序逼迫」嘅語氣將人拖入轉帳或提供資料嘅陷阱。當受害者喺手機螢幕上一眼見到「INTERPOL」字樣就即刻相信，責任其實唔只落喺騙徒，仲包括平台風控、廣告審批同資訊核實嘅速度同準繩。

更值得深思嘅，係呢類詐騙為何可以反覆出現、甚至擴散到同一地區、同一受害族群。社會上常見嘅誤區係話「騙得咁多，證明打擊唔夠」。但單靠事後封號未必夠，因為騙局往往係流水線：域名、文案、受眾定向、支付路徑都可迅速更換。若平台對高風險名詞（例如國際組織、執法機構、政治人物）冇更嚴格嘅真偽核驗，亦冇針對「冒充機構」建立更即時嘅封堵機制，就算偶爾清走一批廣告，也可能只係拖延下一輪上架。

政府同監管機構亦應由此抽取教訓：打擊詐騙要更聚焦於「供應鏈」。例如要求平台對冒充特定機構嘅廣告設立更高門檻（包括更即時嘅審批、被舉報後嘅處理時限、以及可追溯嘅廣告主資料），並強化與本地執法部門嘅資料交換；同時，亦要投放資源令市民明白「即使看見國際機構字眼，都唔等於真」。喺公共教育層面，與其單向宣傳「小心詐騙」，不如針對呢類冒充執法機構嘅具體話術，教大家如何核實：例如要求任何「跟進案件」都要有可驗證嘅官方渠道，而唔係只憑短訊、廣告或私人訊息推進。

至於立場方面，我認為今次 Meta 的移除行動係正確方向，亦證明媒體追查可以促成平台快速處理；但真正嘅成果，應該量化同制度化，而唔係靠偶發事件「清一清」。香港作為國際城市，詐騙手法愈來愈科技化、跨平台化，監管與平台必須由被動回應升級到主動防範：用更嚴密風控阻斷起手式，用更快核實阻截擴散，用更清晰責任追蹤降低僥倖。當平台能夠更快、更準地處理冒充廣告，受害者先有喘息空間；而社會亦先有能力把打擊詐騙由「亡羊補牢」推向「防患未然」。
zh.topic_title: Meta removes fake INTERPOL ads targeting Hong Kong scam victims
